# Current State

Fast project orientation — reads live state from git and existing docs, synthesizes a
concise report. Pure read: no code changes, no file writes, no tests.

## Step 1 — Detect Project Structure

Check for these state documents in order:

| Priority | File | What it tells you |
|----------|------|--------------------|
| 1 | `CURRENT_STATE.md` | Explicit shipped/next state |
| 2 | `CHANGELOG.md` / `CHANGELOG` | Shipped history |
| 3 | `docs/ROADMAP.md` / `ROADMAP.md` | Planned work |
| 4 | `README.md` | Project overview + status badges |

Note which exist. If none exist, rely entirely on git history.

## Step 2 — Read Live Git State

Git is the primary dependency. Use `wfc git` if available; fall back to bare git if not.

```bash
# Preferred (WFC available)
wfc git log 10          # last 10 commits
wfc git status          # uncommitted changes
wfc git branches        # active local branches

# Fallback (bare git)
git log --oneline -10
git status --short
git branch -v
```

If git is not available at all, stop and tell the user — the skill cannot run without it.

## Step 3 — Read State Docs

Read whichever state docs exist (Step 1). Extract three things:

- **Shipped** — what's declared done (most recent first)
- **In flight** — active branches, WIP sections, ongoing tracks
- **Next** — explicitly planned epics, tasks, or tracks

If no state docs exist, infer all three from git log and branch names.

## Step 4 — Staleness Check

Compare git log against the "Shipped" or equivalent section of any state doc.

Mark **STALE** if:
- Commits exist whose content isn't reflected in the state doc
- "What's Next" items appear done per git log
- The state doc's "last session" date is older than the most recent commit date

Mark **FRESH** if the state doc reflects the git log reasonably well.

## Step 5 — Write the Report

Always write `CURRENT_STATE.md` at the project root — create it if absent, overwrite it if present. Then print the same content to screen.

```markdown
# {project-name} — Current State

**Branch:** `{branch}` | **Last updated:** {date} | **Tests:** {N passing if known}

---

## Shipped

### {Most Recent Batch/Epic Name} (merged — {date or PR ref if available})

- {bullet: what shipped}
- {bullet: what shipped}

(Repeat for up to 3 prior batches/epics. Older history lives in git log.)

---

## What's Next

{Track A — description}: {one-line summary of work}

{Track B — description}: {one-line summary of work}

---

## In Flight

{Only include if there are active non-main branches or uncommitted changes}
- `{branch-name}` — {what it does, inferred from branch name + commits}
- Uncommitted: {summary of wfc git status / git status --short}

---

## Backlog

{Items that are planned but not actively in flight. Pull from any existing ROADMAP or prior CURRENT_STATE.md backlog section.}
```

Omit sections that have no content. Keep Shipped bullets tight — one line per item.

## Step 6 — Commit the File

After writing, stage and commit:

```bash
# WFC
wfc git add CURRENT_STATE.md
wfc git commit 'docs: update CURRENT_STATE.md'

# Bare git fallback
git add CURRENT_STATE.md
git commit -m 'docs: update CURRENT_STATE.md'
```

Then print: "CURRENT_STATE.md updated and committed."

---

## What NOT To Do

- Don't write code or make non-documentation changes
- Don't run tests or builds
- Don't run long-running commands (swift build, npm test, etc.)
- Don't hallucinate project status — if a section has no data, omit it or say "unknown"
- Don't skip the commit step — the file on disk is the deliverable
